los.text: Describe the psychological, social and behavioural factors that influence patterns of self-harm and suicide
los.html:
Psychological
  • Mental disorder (present in ~90% of suicides: depression, bipolar, schizophrenia, personality disorder, eating disorders, PTSD)
  • Hopelessness (strong predictor), entrapment and defeat, impulsivity, perfectionism, poor problem-solving, emotional dysregulation, low self-esteem, previous trauma/childhood abuse.
Social
  • Social isolation
  • Living alone
  • Bereavement
  • Relationship breakdown
  • Unemployment/debt
  • Homelessness
  • Imprisonment
  • Bullying (including online)
  • Discrimination (LGBTQ+)
  • Being a veteran
  • Certain occupations with access to means (doctors, vets, farmers)
  • Exposure to suicide of others (contagion, irresponsible media reporting).
Behavioural
  • Previous self-harm (strongest predictor: ~50–100× risk in following year)
  • Alcohol and drug misuse (disinhibition)
  • Access to lethal means
  • Recent discharge from psychiatric inpatient care (first weeks highest risk)
  • Not engaging with services
  • Impulsive acts.
Physical illnessChronic pain, disability, terminal illness, recent diagnosis (cancer, HIV, MS).
ProtectiveSocial support, children at home, religious/cultural beliefs, problem-solving skills, engagement with care, restricted access to means.
ModelsStress–diathesis; Integrated Motivational–Volitional model (O'Connor): defeat/humiliation → entrapment → suicidal ideation → action (volitional moderators: access to means, impulsivity, exposure).

los.text: Describe the presentation and emergency treatment of self-poisoning
los.html:
Common agents (UK)Paracetamol (commonest), NSAIDs, antidepressants (SSRIs; TCAs most dangerous), benzodiazepines, opioids, alcohol (often co-ingested); also salicylates, lithium, iron, insulin, recreational drugs.
Assessment
  • ABCDE
  • What, how much (mg/kg), when (single vs staggered), co-ingestants
  • GCS, pupils, RR, HR/BP, temperature, glucose, ECG (QRS/QT).
  • Bloods: paracetamol and salicylate levels (all overdoses), U&E, LFT, INR, glucose, VBG (acid–base, lactate), CK.
  • Use TOXBASE / National Poisons Information Service.
GeneralSupportive care; activated charcoal within 1 h for adsorbable drugs (not iron, lithium, alcohol); airway protection.
PoisonFeaturesTreatment
ParacetamolOften asymptomatic early; RUQ pain, vomiting; liver failure 2–4 days (NAPQI depletes glutathione)
  • IV acetylcysteine if level above the treatment line (4–15 h), staggered/unknown timing, or >150 mg/kg presenting >8 h.
  • Liver unit if ↑INR, acidosis, ↑creatinine (King's College criteria)
OpioidsPinpoint pupils, ↓RR, ↓GCSNaloxone (titrate; short half-life → may need infusion)
TCAsAnticholinergic, ↓BP, seizures, broad QRS, arrhythmiasIV sodium bicarbonate; avoid flumazenil
BenzodiazepinesSedationSupportive; flumazenil rarely (seizure risk)
SalicylatesTinnitus, vomiting, hyperventilation (resp alkalosis → metabolic acidosis)Fluids, urinary alkalinisation, haemodialysis if severe
Iron, lithiumGI, neurotoxicityDesferrioxamine / haemodialysis
  • After medical treatment: psychosocial assessment by mental health/liaison team before discharge (NICE NG225) for everyone presenting with self-harm.

los.text: Describe the epidemiology of suicidal behaviour and outline patient risk assessment strategies
los.html:
UK figures
  • ~6,000–7,000 suicides/year
  • ~¾ male
  • Highest rates in men aged 45–54 (middle-aged)
  • Rising in young people.
  • Wales has higher rates than the England average.
  • Self-harm is far more common (10–20× suicides), especially in young women aged 16–24.
MethodsHanging/strangulation (commonest), poisoning (commonest method of self-harm), jumping, drowning.
TrendsFell after domestic gas detoxification (1960s) and paracetamol pack-size limits (1998): means restriction works.
Risk assessment approach (NICE NG225, 2022)
  • Don't use risk tools/scales (e.g. SAD PERSONS) to predict suicide or decide who gets treatment or discharge: they have poor predictive value.
  • Do a needs-based psychosocial assessment: understand the person's history, current difficulties, mental state, intent (planning, final acts, precautions against discovery, lethality belief), method, protective factors, safeguarding (children, dependants), and what help they want.
  • Ask directly about suicidal thoughts (asking does not increase risk).
  • Collaborative safety plan: warning signs, coping strategies, contacts (Samaritans 116 123), restricting access to means, follow-up arrangements.
  • Involve family/carers where appropriate; consider confidentiality limits.

los.text: Describe the connection between the epidemiology of suicidal behaviour and the assessment of risk and patient need
sessions: MHS 1: Epidemiology of suicide and self-harm
los.html:
Epidemiology identifies groups at higher risk
  • Men
  • Middle age
  • Previous self-harm
  • Mental illness
  • Recent psychiatric discharge
  • Substance misuse
  • Unemployment/debt
  • Isolation
  • LGBTQ+
  • Prisoners
  • Certain occupations
  • People in contact with criminal justice
  • Chronic illness.
But the paradox
  • Most people with these risk factors never die by suicide, and many suicides occur in "low-risk" people.
  • So individual prediction is impossible (low base rate → poor positive predictive value).
Implications for assessment
  • Use epidemiological knowledge to raise awareness and inform a needs assessment, not to label someone "low risk" and discharge.
  • Focus on the individual's needs, circumstances and modifiable factors (treat depression, address alcohol, debt advice, social support, safety planning).
  • Static risk factors (sex, history) vs dynamic factors (hopelessness, intoxication, recent loss, access to means) that can change quickly and be targeted.
Population level
  • Epidemiology guides prevention strategies: means restriction (barriers on bridges, pack sizes)
  • Safer media reporting
  • Support after self-harm
  • Targeted programmes (men's sheds, workplace programmes)
  • Crisis services
  • Postvention after suicide clusters.
  • Wales: national strategy (Talk to Me 2 / new suicide and self-harm prevention strategy).

los.text: Describe how psychological, social, and anthropological factors are linked to patterns of self-harm and suicide
los.html:
PsychologicalMental illness, cognitive style (hopelessness, entrapment), impulsivity, emotional pain, coping skills (see LO 1).
Sociological(Durkheim, Le Suicide, 1897)
  • Suicide rates reflect social forces:
  • Egoistic: weak social integration (isolated, single).
  • Altruistic: excessive integration (self-sacrifice for the group).
  • Anomic: weak regulation during social upheaval (economic crises, sudden change).
  • Fatalistic: excessive regulation (prisoners, oppression).
Social trends: recession and austerity linked to rises in suicide; rural isolation; unemployment.
Anthropological/cultural
  • Meanings of suicide and self-harm vary by culture (honour, shame, religion: stigma or prohibition reduces rates/reporting)
  • Gender norms (men less likely to seek help: "masculinity" and stoicism)
  • Methods vary by availability (pesticides in rural Asia)
  • Self-harm as communication of distress or coping (emotion regulation) rather than intent to die
  • Ritual and collective meanings
  • Migration and acculturation stress
  • Indigenous communities affected by colonisation.
ImplicationCulturally competent assessment; avoid stigmatising language ("committed suicide" → "died by suicide"); interventions must fit social context.
